utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Please be seated. Good afternoon. First I would like the registrar to call the case we are hearing today. Mr. Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-02-61-A, the Prosecutor versus Miroslav Deronjic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now ask for the appearances of the parties. The Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. My name is Slobodan Cvijetic. I am an attorney at law. And I am representing the appellant, Mr. Miroslav Deronjic. Next to me is my co-counsel, Mr. Slobodan Zecevic, attorney-at-law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cvijetic. Now for the appearances of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours. I'm Mark McKeon, appearing for the Prosecution. Seated to my right is appeal counsel, Barbara Goy. And to my left is our case manager, Lourdes Galicia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McKeon. Mr. Deronjic, I wanted to make sure that you understand what I'm saying. THE APPELLANT: [Interpretation] Your Honours, good afternoon. I can follow the proceedings well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated. As the registrar announced, the case on our agenda today is the Prosecutor versus Miroslav Deronjic. This is an appeal from the sentencing judgement rendered by the Trial Chamber on 30th March 2004. At the plea hearing held on 30 September 2003, Mr. Deronjic pleaded guilty to one count arising out of events that took place in the Muslim village of Glogova in the Bratunac municipality in Eastern Bosnia and Herzegovina. According to the second amended indictment, Mr. Deronjic was then president of the Bratunac Crisis Staff, participated in the joint criminal enterprise which had as objective the permanent removal by force or other means of Bosnian Muslim inhabitants from the village of Glogova in the municipality of Bratunac. On 9 May 1992, as part of his participation in this joint criminal enterprise, he launched an attack on the village of Glogova. The village was burned down in part and the Bosnian Muslim residents were forcibly displaced from the village. As a result of this attack, 64 Muslim civilians from the village were killed, Bosnian Muslim homes, private property, and the mosque were destroyed, and a substantial part of Glogova was razed to the ground. Based on the plea agreement, the second amended indictment and the factual basis, the Trial Chamber entered a conviction under Article 7(1) of the Statute against Mr. Deronjic for one count of persecutions committed on 9 May 1992, a crime against humanity, pursuant to Article 5(H) of the Statute. On 18 March 2004, the Trial Chamber sentenced Mr. Deronjic, Judge Schomburg dissenting, to 10 years of imprisonment. Mr. Deronjic has appealed his sentence. Today we will hear arguments from both parties, but before giving the floor to counsel, I will summarise briefly the grounds of appeal advanced by the Defence as stated in its written submissions. In his appellant's brief, Mr. Deronjic has raised four grounds of appeal: One, in his first ground of appeal, Mr. Deronjic contends that "The Trial Chamber erred in law and fact and abused its discretion in reaching conclusions and findings which are based upon evidence not specifically contained in the second amended indictment, the plea agreement, or the factual basis. The second ground of appeal is that "The Trial Chamber erred in finding the lex mitior principle is not applicable in Mr. Deronjic's case. In his third ground of appeal, Mr. Deronjic says that "The Trial Chamber erred with respect to the factors it took into account in aggravation." Finally, in his last ground of appeal, Mr. Deronjic alleges that "The Trial Chamber erred when considering the mitigating factors." I will now remind the parties about the standard of review applicable to sentencing appeals. The relevant provisions on sentencing are Articles 23 and 24 of the Statute and the Rules 100 to 106 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. Under Article 25 of the Statute, an appeal is not a trial de novo. The role of the Appeals Chamber is limited to correcting errors of law invalidating a decision and errors of fact that have occasioned a miscarriage of justice. Trial Chambers are vested with broad discretion to tailor the penalties to fit the individual circumstances of the accused and the gravity of the crime. In general, the Appeals Chamber will not revise a sentence unless the Trial Chamber has committed a discernible error in exercising its discretion. A Trial Chamber's decision may, for example, be disturbed on appeal if the appellant shows that the Trial Chamber erred in the weighing process, either by taking into account what it ought not to have considered or by failing to take into account what it ought to have considered. Before we proceed, I will ask the parties to be precise and clear in their presentation of the grounds of appeal and their responses and replies. I will turn now to explain how we are going to proceed during this hearing. Consistent with the order rescheduling the appeal hearing issued on June 7th, the counsel for the Defence: "One, counsel for the Defence shall have up to 30 minutes to make oral submissions. "Two, the Prosecution shall have up to 30 minutes to respond to the Defence's submissions. "Three, the Defence shall have up to ten minutes to reply to the Prosecution's response. "And four, Mr. Deronjic will have ten minutes for a personal statement if he so wishes." So now we turn to the counsel for the Defence. Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours, my learned friends from the Prosecution. I will begin my submissions with a quotation from a book of one of our great writers. Milos Crnjanski, a great writer who for many years lived in exile away from his homeland in a very refined and intelligent way writes about the days and years of his life abroad. And in his book, the novel about London, he says the following: "All writers tend to agree mostly when it comes to the world in which we live. They say that it is some kind of a large, unusual stage on which everyone for a while plays their role, and then they come off the stage never to appear on it again. Never. They neither know why they played in that theatre nor why they had that particular role or who assigned that role to them. The viewers themselves don't know later on where they went after they left the theatre. The writers simply say" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: You have to wait one second. We have a tiny technical problem. Thank you -- you can hear me?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Okay. Now our major technical problems have been resolved and we can proceed. Please, Defence, do continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "They neither know why they played in that theatre nor why they had that particular role or who assigned that role to them. The viewers don't know later on where they went after leaving the theatre. The writers also say that it is only at that particular moment of getting off the stage that all of us are equal, the kings and the beggars." Perhaps these thoughts offered by the writer's pen could be linked with the context of participation in wartime events, which we might find ourselves in and over which we have very little influence or none at all. Simply, these events took place in an area where we lived, on the soil where we had our roots. What the Defence wish to say in this case in a strictly legal sense was stated in our appellant's brief and in the reply to the respondent's brief. In our oral submissions, the Defence will emphasise the following: In our brief, we already pointed out that the Trial Chamber erred because with respect to certain facts and the level of responsibility of the accused it went beyond the plea package, comprised of the second amended indictment, plea agreement, and factual basis, which support the previous two documents. We have already cited parts of the judgement based on which the Defence reached this conclusion. In accordance with the practice of courts in the former SFRY and nowadays in the practice of the courts in the countries created after the dissolution of the former Yugoslavia, the position is that the Court is bound by the indictment and that there must be objective identity between the judgement and the indictment, both with respect to the factual description of a crime and with respect to the legal qualification of an act for which the accused is charged. By applying a narrow interpretation to this concept of objective identity, jurisprudence took the view that the Court is strictly bound by the indictment. If a somewhat broader interpretation is applied, then the Court is authorised to deviate from the factual description of the crime in the indictment and also from the legal qualification of that act but only if it is in favour of the accused. Such position taken in the jurisprudence in our jurisdiction did not foresee a situation in which criminal proceedings could conclude with a guilty plea of the accused reached on the basis of plea bargaining with the Prosecution, because our criminal legislation until recently did not provide for such a situation. However, here before this Tribunal, the situation is much clearer. The Statute provides for a possibility for proceedings to be concluded with an agreement reached between the accused and the Prosecutor, providing that the conditions in Rule 62 bis are met. The Trial Chamber established that the requirements from Rule 62 bis were met after holding several hearings during which all dilemmas were resolved largely on the basis of the facts which were made undisputable by the Prosecution and Defence. Upon completing hearings, while the judgement was drafted, the Trial Chamber went beyond the plea package, thus depriving the Defence of an opportunity to react to that, so that our only avenue was to point that out in our appellant's brief. This act of the Trial Chamber is prejudicial to the accused because by wrongly interpreting certain facts, especially the form of mens rea of the accused, the Trial Chamber increased his level of responsibility, which eventually had an impact on the severity of the sentence. The establishment of the Tribunal at the highest international level implies the application of highest judicial standards, both in view of the application of substantive, criminal, and procedural law. These highest standards necessarily imply the application of progressive institutes and principles of criminal law, including lex mitior, as a universal legal principle. As such, as a universal legal principle, lex mitior constitutes part of the international customary law, which has been recognised by the jurisprudence of the Tribunal as a source of law. The manner in which the Trial Chamber interpreted and implied the lex mitior principle does not uphold the highest judicial standards before the Tribunal. In its appellant's brief, the Defence stated in writing its view with respect to that principle. Furthermore, the manner in which the Trial Chamber established and assessed the aggravating circumstances is neither proper nor in accordance with the case law of the Tribunal, which I hope was sufficiently referred to in our brief. The appellant pled guilty, both in terms of legal qualification as well as in terms of the factual description of his acts. All of the facts admitted by him were included in the crime and represent its integral part. These same facts from special vulnerability of victims to others were taken out of the criminal act by the Trial Chamber and considered separately as aggravating circumstances. This aggravates the crime and the responsibility of the accused beyond the scope to which he pleaded guilty. By doing so, once again, the Trial Chamber went beyond the framework of the plea package, which finally had an impact on the severity of the sentence. Your Honours, it is true that certain parts of the allegations from the fourth ground of appeal have not materialised yet, the ones pertaining to the testimony of the accused Miroslav Deronjic in the Prosecutor versus Oric case, which have been announced by the Defence in accordance with the Rule 115 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. However, that doesn't mean that this testimony will not materialise because this case is currently being tried. It's in progress. So if the Prosecution wishes, it can call the accused to testify. The Prosecution in its response brief disputes the possibility of using additional evidence in the appellant's brief by claiming the following. I quote: "In practical sense, invoking additional evidence which perhaps will never be admitted is problematic." They go on to suggest that the reference or the fact that Rule 115 was invoked ought to be removed from the brief. Your Honours, there is no need to remove this from the brief because in our same brief we explained that this does not constitute new evidence. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. I am quoting now the brief, where we go on to say that "The appellant in his plea agreement has agreed that he would cooperate and testify before and after sentencing," and in that respect his testimony in the Oric case cannot be viewed as new evidence, but it goes on to support the issue of his good character to a great degree because the appellant, even though already sentenced, agrees to undertake and fulfil all obligations with respect to the Prosecution. "While preparing to testify in the said case, the accused gave a very detailed interview to the Prosecution, shedding light on the events in Srebrenica and regarding Srebrenica, providing a lot of new details, so that his mere intention to testify in this case goes to his good character, even though it has not yet been -- it has not yet materialised." Right now there are a number of cases in progress before the Tribunal which are very important and complex and have to do with the events in Srebrenica and that general area. In accordance with the plea agreement, the accused will testify about these events. The accused stands available to the Prosecution in all cases; however, he has no power over the selection made by the Prosecution. Your Honours, the government of Republika Srpska adopted and promulgated last year the report on the events in Srebrenica after many unsuccessful attempts. This time, however, the report was adopted and approved also by the relevant international parties and is being circulated within this Tribunal as well. The technical preparation of this report was done by a special commission of the government. What this Chamber may not know is that the members of this commission, with the consent of the Defence team and the knowledge of the Office of the Prosecutor, spent some time in the UN Detention Unit and took an extensive interview from this accused. The report of the commission adopted by the government of Republika Srpska is largely based on that interview given by the accused. This has initiated positive developments in Republika Srpska which are reflected in the changed attitude of Republika Srpska authorities towards the events in Srebrenica but also in a different approach of the authorities and a large number of the accused towards the Tribunal itself. The intention and desire of the appellant to tell the truth obviously goes beyond the requirements of the Tribunal. Your Honours, the process of rehabilitation is a complex process that has to be customised to the person in order to give adequate effects and in order for the sentence to properly serve the purpose of improving an individual, rather than being just retribution. These are the modern postulates of penal psychology and the associated implementation of the rehabilitation process. Rehabilitation represents a combination of procedures and processes that are geared at enabling an individual to function at his maximum possible level in view of his actual capacities and potential. All this taken together leads to socially desirable changes in attitudes, values, and the conduct of persons. In terms of personality, not all perpetrators of criminal acts, including the gravest crimes, qualified as serious violations of international humanitarian law, such as war crimes, are the same. For the same or similar crime, the purpose of punishment can be achieved with sentences of different severity. The basic parameter that dictates different sentences lies precisely in the possibility of rehabilitation or the ability of rehabilitation of an accused. In terms of type of personality, that process goes slowly with some perpetrators and more quickly in others. Miroslav Deronjic is a sensitive type of person with adequate capacity to adjust to varying conditions of life and a very good intellectual potential that guides him in his thoughts and the process of making conclusions. Having achieved the goals he intimately set himself, he got a confirmation of his values in parenthood; however, the cruel onset of war and the associated events damaged his family in many ways. The marital relationship was disturbed. The family began to drift apart and to lose its mutual emotional and communication capacity, which affected each of them individually, causing deep emotional suffering and pain. Information available from expert literature, both in our country and throughout the world, indicate that in penal conditions persons with this type of personality tend to become even more sensitive, to withdraw into their own world and thoughts, unless they are given sufficient social support and appreciation. This can be an introduction into some more serious psychological or psychiatric disorder, which is currently absent in Miroslav Deronjic, but always continues to be a real threat with such sensitive, intellectually superior persons. The purpose of sentencing in the case of Miroslav Deronjic can be achieved by integrating all three aspects of punishment: Deterrence, retribution, and last but not the least, rehabilitation. A sentence of 10 years' imprisonment is dominated by deterrence and retribution. But if we were to take into account the rehabilitation of Miroslav Deronjic, in whose case this process began significantly earlier than his arrest, back in 1997, when he had his first contacts with the Office of the Prosecutor, and has continued successfully to this day, we have good reason to conclude that in the case of Miroslav Deronjic the purpose of punishment can be attained even with a milder sentence than that meted out by the Trial Chamber. Your Honours, in the desire to emphasise the issue of rehabilitation of the appellant, we asked psychologist Ana Najman to provide additional clarification to her psychological expertise already done during the trial, during the procedure before the Trial Chamber. Mrs. Ana Najman kindly granted our request and made additional clarifications of the psychological expertise, emphasising rehabilitation as an important segment of the purpose of punishment. This clarification is attached to our contribution and forms an integral part of it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Counsel for the Defence. I will now turn to the Prosecution. Mr. McKeon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. I will be addressing this morning the first and the fourth ground of appeal. My colleague, Ms. Barbara Goy, will be addressing the second and third ground of appeal. The way we intend to proceed this morning is I will start with the first ground of appeal. I will then turn over the podium to Ms. Goy, and then I will resume the podium and conclude our argument with the fourth ground of appeal. On the first ground of appeal, Your Honour, this ground raises two legal issues and various alleged factual issues. The first legal issue is whether the Trial Chamber erred in going beyond what has been designated as the plea agreement package in establishing the factual basis for the guilty plea. The second legal issue is whether the Trial Chamber then erred in using this evidence in establishing Mr. Deronjic's sentence. Your Honour, we believe that these two legal issues can be quickly disposed of. As to the first issue, the accused was not convicted of any offence that was not contained in the second amended indictment, was not convicted of any persecutory acts that were not contained within the second amended indictment. In fact, the accused seems to accept this -- rather, I should say Mr. Deronjic, who is no longer the accused, now the convicted -- seems to receive this because his argument is that the Trial Chamber should not have gone beyond the factual basis, as opposed to going beyond the indictment. Secondly, Your Honour, there's nothing, as we've pointed out in our filings, in the Rules or the plea agreement that limits a Chamber taking a guilty plea from considering evidence beyond the written factual basis in deciding whether to accept that guilty plea. And third, Your Honour, it is difficult to see where there would be any prejudice on this legal issue because ultimately what happened is the Trial Chamber accepted the guilty plea, which is what Mr. Deronjic wanted to take place. The second legal issue is whether, having accepted that guilty plea, the evidence could then be accepted in sentencing. And here there's a similar result. And I'd like to make two points. The first was made in our brief, which is that there's nothing in the Rules or the plea agreement that purports to limit a Trial Chamber to looking at only agreed facts in setting a sentence in a guilty-plea situation. In fact, Rule 100 seems to contemplate expressly the opposite, which is that they may consider any relevant information submitted by the parties. My second point, Your Honour, is taken from the more recent decision in Dragan Nikolic, which occurred after we filed our brief. In that case, this Chamber held that Mr. Nikolic had waived his objection to the contemplation of this evidence by not raising it at the Trial Chamber. We have a similar situation in this case. Here the evidence was not only put in in some cases by the Prosecution without objection from Mr. Deronjic, but in many cases was actually put in by Mr. Deronjic himself. There was no objection to the evidence when it was put before the Court. There was no objection to this evidence at the conclusion of the initial sentencing hearing and their submissions. When it came to the renewed sentencing hearing in early March, the Trial Chamber actually observed that it would be using this evidence in part to be determining the sentence. That's on page 250 of the transcript. There was no objection then. And when additional evidence was put in by the Prosecution from various trials, again there was no objection. It was only at the closing submissions of the -- of Mr. Deronjic that there was anything approaching an objection to this evidence, and that's at page 336 of the transcript, where he notes that this evidence, which in that case he concluded the interview of Mr. Deronjic should only -- the Court should be limited to the plea-agreement package and the testimony of Mr. Deronjic determining culpability and sentence. Our submission, Your Honour, is that that is not an objection that preserved this issue, that in effect it was argument; it was not asking the Trial Chamber to do anything; and in fact under the circumstances made no sense because if the evidence could only -- could not be heard on culpability and could not be used for sentencing, the question is then: What could the evidence be used for? There's nothing else. And, in fact, the Trial Chamber properly considered this evidence. On the factual issues, Your Honour, there's a number of factual errors that were allegedly made. I do not intend to go into those in my submissions except in response to questions. I did want to make two observations though: The first observation is at one point the Trial Chamber said that most of its factual conclusions were based on the agreed facts. This reference, we submit, should be construed as meaning the facts not only in the factual basis but also the facts that were agreed by the parties during the sentencing hearing. If you go through the transcript, you will see that Judge Schomburg repeatedly asked the Prosecution and then the Defence whether a certain characterisation of the facts were correct, and they would then agree to those facts. So when he refers to the agreed facts, he's referring to not only what in the factual basis but also to the agreements reached by the parties during the hearing. The second observation, Your Honour, is with respect to Mr. Deronjic's interview. We had cited in our submissions in our brief in a few places references to Mr. Deronjic's interview. Our view was that this did not violate the understanding with Mr. Deronjic that this information would not be used to his detriment because he had, in fact, put this information into evidence himself, and therefore it was not the Prosecution who was tendering the evidence. It was Mr. Deronjic. And the Trial Chamber was entitled to use that evidence. Although we still hold to that legal view, Your Honour, upon reviewing the transcript, it appears that the Trial Chamber may have had a different view. In fact, at one point the Trial Chamber observed that it could not consider this evidence to Mr. Deronjic's detriment in determining the sentence, so it would appear that the Trial Chamber itself did not use Mr. Deronjic's interview in -- in deciding what sentence to give to him, and so we think it would be appropriate for this Chamber to also review the record outside of that evidence. I'm happy to respond to any questions now, or we can respond at the conclusion of our total remarks, if that would be preferable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Do any of my colleagues wish to answer questions now? I see there are none. So you are going to deal with the second ground of appeal and the third ground?

utterances.speaker: MS. GOY
utterances.text: Yes. Good afternoon, Your Honour. I will be addressing the second and the third ground of appeal. The appellant in the second ground of appeal alleges that the Trial Chamber erred in finding that the principle of lex mitior is not applicable in this case with regard to the law in the former Yugoslavia. It is now settled in the jurisprudence of this Tribunal that it is not bound by the principle of lex mitior. This has been held by the Appeals Chamber in the Blaskic and the Dragan Nikolic case. The Blaskic appeal judgement, in footnote 1.433, stated that - I quote - "The International Tribunal is not bound to apply the more lenient penalty under the jurisdiction on the territory of the former Yugoslavia (the lex mitior principle)." This was confirmed by the Appeals Chamber in the Dragan Nikolic case in paragraphs 77 through 86 of the judgement. It is explained there that "It is an inherent element of the principle of lex mitior that the relevant law must be binding upon the Court" because it is only where it is binding that the defendant has a protected legal position. However, the Tribunal is not bound by the law of the former Yugoslavia. It has merely to take it into consideration. Moreover, otherwise, the states in the former Yugoslavia would have the power to undermine the sentencing discretion of the ICTY Judges by simply reducing the national sentencing ranges. This would be incompatible with the Tribunal's primacy provided for in Article 9 of the Statute. Therefore, the Trial Chamber did not commit an error by not applying the principle of lex mitior. This concludes my submissions on the second ground of appeal, and Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. unless Your Honours have questions, I would move on to the third ground of appeal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOY
utterances.text: In his third ground of appeal, the appellant raises legal errors with regard to the five aggravating factors determined by the Trial Chamber in paragraph 222 of the judgement in addition to the error already treated by my colleague, which relates to the plea-agreement package. I will first address general issues which apply to all five aggravating factors and then address specific points with regard to the individual aggravating factors. First to the general issues. There are four different errors which the Trial Chamber allegedly committed with regard to one or several of the aggravating factors and which have just been repeated by the counsel for the appellant. Allegedly the Trial Chamber erred by taking into account: One, factors which as such cannot be taken into account in aggravation; two, factors which were part of the factual basis; three, factors which constitute an element of the offence; and, four, factors which were already subsumed in the overall gravity of the offence. The main question here is whether the Trial Chamber impermissibly counted factors twice. It is impermissible to consider circumstances which form an element of the crime as an aggravating factor and it is impermissible to consider a circumstance as an aggravating factor which has already been dealt with to determine the gravity of the crime. As it is apparent from footnote 289, the Trial Chamber was well aware of this principle, as it stated - I quote - "Each circumstance may only justly be considered once." And it is our submission that the Trial Chamber did not violate this principle. The mere fact that the Trial Chamber considered the gravity and the aggravating factors together under one heading in paragraph 178 and following does not mean that it considered the factors twice. It is clear from paragraphs 184, 185, and 223 that the Trial Chamber looked at both the gravity of the crime and the aggravating circumstances. Whether it gave the correct label to each of them - meaning, whether it called them an aggravating factor - or used it to determine the gravity of the crime is in our submission irrelevant as long as when determining the aggravating factors it only took into account factors which can be taken into account in aggravation, which do not constitute an element of the crime, and as long as it did not take the factors into account twice for sentencing. I would now like to address the individual aggravating factors. The first is the large number of victims. The large number of victims can be considered as an aggravating factor because persecution does not require a large number of victims, so it is not an element of persecution as such. And it is the fact that the acts of the accused must be part of a widespread or systematic attack does not mean that the large number of victims cannot constitute an aggravating factor. It is correct that the widespread nature refers to the large-scale nature and the number of the targeted persons, but it is not required that the accused himself is individually responsible for the large number of victims. Here, however, he is as a co-perpetrator in the joint criminal enterprise responsible for having committed crimes against a large number of victims. Therefore, this additional factor can be taken into account as an aggravating factor, and it has not been considered by the Trial Chamber to determine the gravity, but clearly, as can be seen from paragraph 222, as an aggravating factor. With regard to the second aggravating factor, the launching of a meticulously planned attack. We would like to note in addition to what we have argued in our response brief that the Trial Chamber for the second factor also used the word "launching," which indicates setting the plan or attack in motion. Both parts, the launching and the planning, could be used as an aggravating factor. Mr. Deronjic not only decided to attack Glogova and participated in the planning of this operation but also launched the attack in the sense that he ordered the attack to start. His involvement in the planning and the launching of the attack do not constitute necessary elements of the crime of persecution or the mode of liability of joint criminal enterprise. Joint criminal enterprise requires acting on the basis of a common plan, but it does not require a phase of meticulous planning. Moreover, as the Kvocka Appellate Chamber has held, it only requires "a contribution," not even a significant or substantial contribution. And therefore this very substantial contribution by the appellant could be considered as an aggravating factor. And planning is not a necessary element of the systematic attack either. A plan or policy is not a legal element of a crime against humanity. And, moreover, it is not required that the defendant personally was involved in the planning. His acts do only need to be part of the systematic attack. The appellant did not demonstrate that the launching of the meticulously planned attack was taken into account to determine the gravity of the crime and therefore failed to demonstrate that the Trial Chamber erred by considering it an aggravating factor. With regard to the third aggravating factor, the abuse of the position of authority, I would like to refer Your Honours to our response brief in paragraphs 4.76 and following. With regarding the fourth aggravating factor, the ordering of additional torching, it is our submission that the Trial Chamber did not err when it considered the ordering of additional torching as an aggravating factor. Similar to the aggravating factor just discussed, the ordering of additional torching constitutes another increase in the personal involvement of the accused more than just a contribution to the joint criminal enterprise, and therefore it was not a necessary element of the offence. And it is obvious from paragraph 202 of the judgement that the Trial Chamber considered it as an aggravating factor and not as part of the gravity. Regarding the last aggravating factor, the special vulnerability and defencelessness of the victim, we have set out in paragraphs 4.87 and 4.88 of the brief that the vulnerability of the victim is a factor which is accepted as aggravating in the jurisprudence of the Tribunal. It does not constitute an element of the crime, as the jurisprudence of this Tribunal distinguishes between the status of being a civilian, which constitutes an element of the crime against humanity, and the special vulnerability of the victim, which does not constitute an element. The cumulative effect of being disarmed and the false promise of safety put the victims here in a much more vulnerable position than the ordinary civilian. The Trial Chamber did consider this as an aggravating factor and did not subsume it in the gravity of the offence, as in paragraph 209, it concludes - I quote - "It has to be considered an aggravation of the sentence." This ends my submission, and I'm available for your questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Goy. [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Oh, sorry. What did you miss? I am sure nothing very important. Thank you very much. I don't see any questions from my distinguished colleagues. Mr. McKeon.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOY
utterances.text: Then I will pass on to my colleague. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you for the presentation on the fourth ground of appeal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: We'll rearrange our furniture here again, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: We will rearrange our furniture here again. I will be brief, Your Honour. On the fourth ground of appeal, it is claimed that there were errors with respect to four mitigating factors: Concerns expressed about the truthfulness of Mr. Deronjic's admissions; rehabilitation as a sentencing principle; the character and behaviour of the accused; and his family circumstances. It is alleged that with respect to each of these that was legal error and factual error. I think we can dispose of the legal error question quite easily and quickly, Your Honours. As to the first, the accused -- Mr. Deronjic does not argue that if he had in fact been found to be untruthful in his admissions, that this could eliminate the possibility to consider his admissions in mitigation. In other words, if -- if he were lying, he doesn't argue that it would be improper for the Trial Chamber to take that into account in determining the value of his cooperation. So, in fact, there has been no legal error alleged. As to the second claim on rehabilitation, in fact the Trial Chamber did recognise that rehabilitation was an appropriate sentencing principle, that it should be given some weight but not undue weight, and the fact that it only gave this principle a tertiary importance to deterrence and retribution is consistent with the Celebici appeal, judgement paragraph 806. As to the third claim on character and behaviour, the Trial Chamber in fact did recognise that character and behaviour of the accused can be a mitigating factor, and so there was no error. In fact, they did consider it. And finally, on the fourth claim, the judgement again specifically noted that the accused's family and social situation is a recognised mitigating circumstance and indeed the Trial Chamber took his family circumstances into account --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you slow down a little, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: -- in determining whether or not and how much weight they would give to his cooperation. So we submit, Your Honour, that with respect to the mitigating factors, there was no legal error. As to the question of whether there was a factor error, again, we submit there was none. As to the first factor, the truthfulness of the accused, this is based on paragraph 135 of the judgement. If you review that paragraph, however, you will see that it is only expressing general observations of the Trial Chamber on possible problems in guilty-plea situations. It is not saying that those problems had manifested themselves in this particular case. Indeed, later in the judgement, in paragraphs 252 and 253, they determined that all material discrepancies and inconsistencies had, in fact, been clarified and resolved. So there were no legal errors -- or no factual errors here. On the second factor, of rehabilitation, again, the Trial Chamber did consider this evidence. They, in fact, commissioned a report from an expert in psychology on the accused's socialisation. This report was admitted into evidence and considered by the Trial Chamber. We would note in passing, Your Honour, that that is, in fact, however, a different report than the report that was brought forward by Mr. Deronjic this morning -- or this afternoon. Although we were provided with a copy of this last week, it is our submission that this is not properly before the Appeals Chamber because there has been no motion made to admit this new -- what is in fact a new expert-opinion report. But in any event, Your Honour, the question is did the Trial Chamber consider the possibility of rehabilitation, and they did. On the third factor, the Trial Chamber, in fact, did consider evidence of the accused's good character but did what Trial Chambers are supposed to do, which is to weigh that against the other evidence that it saw of the accused's poor character. Recall, Your Honours, that the Trial Chamber had Mr. Deronjic testify before it for almost a full day and had him at sentencing hearings for several days, so it was able to observe his demeanour and observe his testimony and review his testimony. And we would submit there was no factual error in its determination that when weighed -- when striking the balance, which the Trial Chamber is specially placed to make, that it did not commit any errors. And finally, Your Honour, as to his family situation, there was no factual error in this case because the Trial Chamber did, in fact, consider his family situation and, in fact, gave him credit for it when it considered the value of his cooperation. Had it given the accused -- appellant additional credit for that as a separate factor, that in fact could have been error because it would have been in that case double-counting of the same factor. That concludes our prepared submissions, Your Honour, and we're now prepared to answer any questions that you may have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Do my colleagues have any questions? The Defence, do you have -- Mr. Cvijetic, you may have up to ten minutes to respond to the Prosecution, if you wish. Mr. Cvijetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Yes, I will respond briefly to the submissions made by the Prosecution, and I will say something that has not been said so far. Your Honours, if you read the reply of the Prosecution carefully, you will see in one part of their submissions that the Prosecution does not deny the fact that the Trial Chamber went beyond the plea package; meaning, the second amended indictment, the plea agreement, and the factual basis. They went beyond precisely in the segment which is very important, and that is the form of his culpability or the term that is used here, "mens rea." Therefore, the Prosecution acknowledges this fact in their brief; namely, that the Trial Chamber went beyond the plea package determining a higher level of mens rea than what was contained in the plea package. We believe that this fact, that the Trial Chamber went beyond the framework of the plea package, is quite a considerable one, both when it comes to mens rea and when it comes to the factual description of the crime. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. The fact that the accused pleaded guilty to present a typical case of dolus eventualis. However, the Trial Chamber goes on to interpret his plea and sees or deems his plea as dolus directus, which is not what he pleaded to. This results in the -- in the interpretation or in the view that his crimes were much graver than what he pleaded to, which in the end resulted in a much more severe sentence. Finally, Your Honour, in the sentencing hearing, both the Prosecution and the Defence made the majority of the facts undisputable. The Trial Chamber accepted those facts, did not go on to determine new facts but interpreted the established facts in a different way, not in a reasonable way which would lead to a reasonable conclusion. The Trial Chamber interprets these facts in the same manner it used when it assigned a higher level of culpability to the accused, which once again brought the same result as in the mens rea case. As for lex mitior, the Defence naturally is aware of the position taken by the Appeals Chamber in the Nikolic case, Dragan Nikolic case. We maintain our position that this is a universal principle which has become a part of international customary law, and thus became a source of law applied here before the Tribunal. What the Defence and the Appeals Chamber agree on is that the manner in which the Trial Chamber interprets this principle, lex mitior principle, is not a proper one. Now, as to whether the Appeals Chamber and the Defence would agree about what the proper position ought to be, this is something that you have to rule on. We hope that you would take or uphold our view. As for counting aggravating circumstances twice, I can say that in our brief we quoted sufficiently from the case law of this Tribunal. For example, the Jokic case, showing that the position in the case law of this Tribunal is clear. What goes to show the gravity of the crime cannot be taken outside that context and viewed separately as an aggravating factor. The Prosecution, both today and in their response to our brief, as well as in the case law, say that the persecution does not have a definite definition, both in terms of how the crime can be committed. There are numerous ways in which this crime can be committed. The appellant pled guilty to this crime, the crime of persecution, by saying that he committed it in the form and in the way as stated very concretely in the second amended indictment, in the plea agreement, and in the factual basis. By pleading to this crime in this way, the appellant determined the elements of his act. The way in which he committed this act became an integral part of the act. Now, one may not take out from this crime one of its constitutive elements and then view it separately as an aggravating factor. So we are not now dealing with an abstract case of persecution. No, we are now discussing a specific crime committed by the appellant. As for mitigating circumstances, I would not like to repeat what is stated in our brief. We believe that all of the mitigating circumstances viewed in previous cases by this Tribunal also exist in the case of this appellant. We made an exhaustive list of this. And I will now say a few words about the report of the psychologist. Mrs. Ana Najman was an expert, a psychologist who testified in this case, and she submitted her report during the sentencing hearing, where she addressed the issue of rehabilitation. At the request of the Defence, she simply clarified that portion of her report, the issue of rehabilitation, without adding anything new which would justify the application of Rule 115 of the Rules of Procedure. So this is not new evidence. This is an addition that was provided to the Prosecution in a timely manner. And I will now suggest a diplomatic solution as well. This clarification is attached to our submissions here, and I invite you to read it. And should you find that there is an element of new evidence in it, then you can disregard it. However, if you take the view that we have taken, I do not see in it anything that should prevent you from taking that into account. In addition, there is another factor: When the Chamber decides on the severity of the sentence, the sentence has to be individualised, which means that it has to be tailored to the type and personality of the accused. This explanation of the expert report, in addition to all other material that you have before you, will assist you in making your ruling. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, the counsel for the Defence. And I would like to salute the parties for their brevity, for the brevity of their argument today, which was very, very helpful. And now I will turn to -- oh, I'm terribly sorry. Judge Guney has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Well, I have one question to the Defence counsel concerning the brief in reply in relation to the fourth ground of appeal. In fact, you said in your brief in reply the dissenting opinion of my eminent colleague Judge Schomburg, and then you come to the conclusion that this opinion - I quote - "Does in fact establish the reasoning which ultimately led to the abuse of discretion of the Trial Chamber in the judgement." Could you please explain how a dissenting opinion of a Judge can show or can establish the reasoning of the Trial Chamber judgement.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I will try to be very brief. The fact is that we, the Defence counsel, cannot avoid the impression that the entire judgement is permeated with the dissenting opinion of Judge Schomburg. If in the plea agreement we and the Prosecution agreed on all facts, if we set limits to the sentence, as recommended, we believe that the dissenting opinion of Judge Schomburg the way it was explained had an impact on the choice of the Trial Chamber made [as interpreted] in determining a ten-year sentence, and this is an illustration of our claims. That is an impression that we had, and we tried to prove by stating all the grounds of appeal that we stated. If the Trial Chamber keeps on going beyond the scope of the plea package, if it determines a higher level of mens rea than the one actually pled, we believe that all points -- that all points to the dissenting opinion of Judge Schomburg.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Judge Guney, it's all right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: It's all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: I will now turn to Mr. Deronjic. I believe, you know, that it is our practice to offer the accused - in fact, in your case, the convicted person - in such circumstances the possibility to make a personal statement. And your Defence counsel indicated that you would like to avail yourself of that opportunity. So I invite you now to make a brief personal statement to the Court. THE APPELLANT: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm certainly not one of those people who had no opportunity to address this Tribunal. I had numerous such opportunities before, and I have reason to believe that I will have many more and that the events in Bratunac and the surrounding area will be discussed many times again throughout the world. You understand that this is not an easy job that you have. Of course, there is a general effort to find out the truth. But the truth is unpleasant to many, and I would -- I would rather not speak today at all. I am sorry that I will take up some of everybody's time today, but I do need to make a couple of points. I understand, Your Honours, the need for tragic events to be viewed from all possible angles in order to assess the gravity and the role of each individual participant in them, but I have the impression that in these efforts we are sometimes actually going further away from the set objective. Of course, I would prefer to be wrong in this impression. Therefore, allow me, Your Honour, to make a couple of points, and I will try to be brief. On the 30th of September, 2003, I pled guilty to the second amended indictment. On the same day, I accepted that all the agreed facts describing the events in Glogova on the 9th of May, 1992, as stated in the second amended indictment, are true. That is what I pled to, and I am not questioning that at this moment. It was observed in my judgement that some facts from the first indictment were given up. They were given up because they were not true and because the Defence had provided substantial evidence that they were not, such as my presence on the spot during the commission of certain crimes. It was not observed, however, that the new amended indictment contains a number of facts that the first one didn't and that I provided to the Prosecution. I provided this evidence because I knew it was going to be tested on many occasions before this Tribunal and in many years to come. I didn't skip over the minutest detail regarding my personal participation, and that is very clear. By doing this, I did not reduce my culpability. On the contrary, I increased it, compared to the facts that the Prosecution already knew. I did that because it was very difficult for me to testify about the guilt of others from the position of culprit. I would have preferred to do that from the position of an innocent person. But all the things I said about my own culpability gives me a certain right to talk about the guilt of others. My position, of course, from the ethical point of view, remains disputable at best. Sometimes I talked about my own culpability so much that it was hardly bearable. Before the Trial Chamber, I also said, among other things, that I was guilty because I did not understand certain things and I should have understood them and was able to understand them. I can go no further in self-incrimination. I have already indulged in it to the point of masochism. But I wish to stress the following: I never had the intent for the killings in Glogova to happen. I did not order them. I did not attend them. And for a long time afterwards, I didn't even know about them. I've said all this many times before. I never recognised or confessed to this because even if I had, it wouldn't have been true. This statement of mine, as many others, has passed numerous tests so far. And if anybody wishes to continue challenging it, they can do so now. I do not wish to cast doubt on any point of the factual basis or paragraph 42, which speaks of the killings. I just wish to stress that between observing that I could have predicted certain things, I could have foreseen them, and saying that I could have prevented them, there is a large difference. I understand that the desire of this Tribunal is to view all things from a variety of aspects, including the aspect of general planning, which undoubtedly determined the course of events. The link between those plans and the actual events constitutes a part of the truth about the past war. I said before this Chamber that in autumn 1991 I was committed to the creation of Republika Srpska. That was a public concept, a public design that was embraced by everybody. But at that time, nobody mentioned the use of force in order to achieve that design. It was on the 8th of May, 1992, that I realised otherwise, when Bosnia was engulfed by war. At that time, in Zvornik, Srebrenica, and Bratunac fighting had been going on for a long time already. One of those municipalities, Srebrenica, is just 3 kilometres away from Bratunac. I was in no way involved in those events. The decision to apply force is linked with the unfolding war in our immediate vicinity, and I have already spoken about that. The use of force had clear restrictions. Of this, too, I have already spoken in detail. Therefore, I wish to underline I have nothing to do with the plans that involved the killings of innocent people, their incarceration, and torture, nor did I have anything to do with the arrival of volunteers to Bratunac, their plans, and their order-givers. On the contrary, I risked my life to prevent their conduct. I drove them out of Bratunac on the 13th of May, 1992, and I was the first to do so in Bosnia and Herzegovina. I publicly condemned them in the summer of 1992 in my only interview given during the war for a local newspaper, calling them the worst names. On the same day, I drove out the commander of the JNA unit that had been present there, because I thought him responsible for the tragic events that occurred. I was the only one in Bosnia and Herzegovina who ordered the expulsion of the Red Berets when in the beginning of 1993 they arrived in Bratunac. All the victims that I knew about in that period, I buried properly, engaging appropriate personnel and professionals. For all these reasons, I was justified in saying that I deeply regret all those innocent victims. Without that, my repentance would not be sincere but hypocritical. Thank you, Your Honours, for your attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated. Yes, thank you, Mr. Deronjic, for your statement. We have come to the end of the arguments in this case, and I would like to express my appreciation to all of you, the parties, counsel, interpreters, and the staff from the court management support section for the assistance given to the Court. The hearing stands adjourned. The Court will consider its verdict, of which you will be notified in due course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Counsel for the Defence, documents to which you alluded somewhat earlier has, of course, not been submitted to the Court. It is not before us. I am not aware of any motion to admit it. And I would be reluctant to admit any documents at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, that's not a problem at all. I've already explained why I was offering for that to be submitted. And it is up for you to decide. Perhaps you can review it subsequently, later on. It's not a problem at all. Your Honours, I apologise, if this is something that you have to decide upon, I am prepared to withdraw it in order not to create any procedural problems for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: I don't believe that the Court should review a document which was not properly submitted to it using proper motions and the Rules, and I would therefore regard the document as not being before us.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I withdraw the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: I am quite sure that the registry will return the document to you in good shape. Thank you. The Court will now rise.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 3.40 p.m.
